items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype
items.summary: This document provides a publication template and metadata structure for a technical blog post focused on building Conversational User Interfaces (CUIs) using AI. It outlines key developer focus areas, product stacks, and approval workflows required for publishing technical content through Google Developer Studio. The framework helps engineers organize their guides and solutions to effectively share AI-driven conversational interface designs with the developer community.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). items.title: DevFest is back!

Under the theme "Build, Secure, Scale," participants gain hands-on experience with Google’s developer stack—including Gemini, Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, and Web MCP—through live workshops and codelabs. The conference focuses on enabling developers to prototype rapidly, ensure secure and private deployments, and leverage production-ready infrastructure.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.

items.title: Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats
items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
items.summary: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications. This update allows developers to route long-lived, bi-directional streams and AI workloads directly through the gateway while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability. Additionally, gateways now feature deterministic default hostnames, simplifying environment provisioning and infrastructure-as-code management.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
items.summary: Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), BigQuery, and a four-gate defense-in-depth security stack (Model Armor, Cloud KMS, Binary Authorization, and OPA) to build governed, self-evolving AI agents that remediate live production outages in 1.8 seconds.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Keep a 50% Margin on an AI Subscription: Per-User Cost Caps That Actually Bind
items.summary: If you sell a monthly plan that talks to large language models, the user who loves the product is the one who can wipe out your margin. A “fair use” sentence in the terms does not stop a model bill. You need a ceiling in code, denominated in the same dollars the provider charges you, and you need that ceiling to be a hard stop — not a polite downgrade that keeps spending. I built this for Plenifa, a bilingual AI life coach and language tutor. This is a write-up of the metering design in the running app, not a pitch for the product. Every metered action writes a row with two dollar amounts: Real cost — what the model provider billed, in USD. Charged amount — real cost multiplied by a tier multiplier, which is what draws down the user’s plan allowance. Cheap “economy” models are charged at 1×. Mid-range “standard” models are 1.2×, “premium” 1.5×, and “frontier” 2×. The multiplier is a product choice: a user who picks a costly model burns the visible allowance faster, while the hard cap (described below) still counts real dollars. items.title: I Built a Candle That Burns Down in Real-Time as the Year Passes
items.summary: Hi everyone! I'm Marcos, an independent digital creator from Venezuela. Today I want to share a small project I built entirely from scratch: a web page where a candle slowly consumes itself second by second, showing exactly how much time is left until the New Year. I wanted to create something visual, calming, and slightly philosophical — a way to feel the year passing by instead of just reading a countdown. So I built The Year Candle: a single web page where a green candle with a golden holder burns down mathematically, in perfect sync with the calendar. The math is simple but elegant. The script calculates the percentage of the year that has already passed (from January 1st to December 31st) and applies that percentage to the height of the candle. Every second, the candle shrinks a tiny bit. By the time December 31st at 11:59:59 PM arrives, the candle is completely gone. The best part? It works automatically for every visitor in their own local timezone. Someone in Tokyo, someone in Madrid, and someone in Caracas all see the candle burning according to their own clock. items.summary: I make Smashy Crossroads: Mega Pileup, a car-crash game about one junction and a lot of rush-hour traffic. You drag back, let go, and try to wreck as many cars as you can in a single launch. It's free, it has no ads, there's nothing to buy, and it plays offline. The 3D edition runs in the browser on three.js, and it's coming to Google Play in December. This first devlog is about the smallest system in the game that matters most: the chain timer. It's the thing that makes the second crash worth more than the first. Every wreck is a link in a chain. If the next wreck lands before a short timer runs out, the chain grows. It comes from the difficulty table, so it isn't one fixed value: Easy gives you six seconds, Medium five, Hard four. Medium is the default. Each extra link adds half again of the base cash. items.title: How I worked out Palworld's exact Pal stat formula, and checked it in game
items.summary: 2,310 stat values, confirmation runs locked in before checking, and one rounding detail most estimates miss Every Pal in Palworld has hidden talent values (the community calls them IVs). Players want to know what their Pal really has, so they can decide which one to breed from. The question sounds simple: given a Pal's level, talent, stars, Souls, trust and passives, what HP, Attack and Defense does the game show? The usual answer is a decimal formula, something like stat * (1 + passive / 100) and then round. It is close. It is also wrong in a lot of small places, and small is enough when you want to recover a hidden number from a displayed one. I wanted the exact version, so I worked it out and then checked it against the game. Two things. First, float32. Every step of the calculation behaves like a 32-bit float, and each step rounds on its own. Decimal constants such as 0.075 or 0.01 are not exact in float32. A percentage like 5% becomes 104.99999237060546875, not 105. When the true answer sits on a rounding boundary, a decimal formula lands on the wrong side. Second, order. items.title: Four things Cloudflare's email handler did that I didn't expect
items.summary: Send one message to two addresses that belong to the same mailbox, and your email() handler runs twice. Same Message-ID, same body, same sender. Only message.to differs. I'm building a small open-source mail app, still in early development, that runs on Cloudflare Workers. Mail comes in through Email Routing's email() handler and goes out through the Email Service send_email binding. Unit tests with made-up messages told me nothing about what follows. Real mail did. Email Routing hands each recipient its own copy. That fits SMTP, where each RCPT TO is its own delivery, but I had been thinking of "a message" as one thing. The handler is also at-least-once: a slow handler is cancelled and run again, and a sender retries after a temporary refusal. So I already had a rule that the same message twice is kept once. The key is a hash of the mailbox and the Message-ID, From, Date and Subject, and when two messages share a key I compare the bodies too, so that someone who guesses a message's headers can't get a real one dropped. items.title: Structuring Research and Academic Writing: The Dual-App Architecture of Prism AI
items.summary: Structuring Research and Academic Writing: The Dual-App Architecture of Prism AI When building a desktop workspace for technical writing, monolithic architectures often become bloated and hard to maintain. Research, chatting with AI, compiling LaTeX documents, and managing references have entirely different UI states and performance profiles. For Prism AI, I chose a dual-app architecture: Prism Chat and Prism Studio. Prism Chat is optimized for conversational context, prompt management, markdown note-taking, and source organization. Its state revolves around chat histories, vector embeddings (locally managed), and unstructured notes. Prism Studio is engineered for structured academic documents. It handles LaTeX syntax highlighting, BibTeX reference parsing, real-time previewing, and PDF compilation via Tectonic. Separating these concerns keeps memory usage lean and allows each module to focus on its specific domain without cross-contaminating UI rendering loops. Explore the code structure on GitHub. items.title: Setup Script to Create Named Transformations — Apply Them to Every Upload
items.summary: The page says marketplace listing images are backing up. In a Node.js service, the safe pattern is to create each named transformation in a setup script, then apply that existing name to every upload; the on-call should never see request retries creating configuration. TL;DR: Create each named image transformation once during deployment, verify in CI that every expected name exists, and make each upload path reference that name. Keep moderation as a separate, explicit gate before an optimized image becomes servable. This is the least complex pattern that prevents request traffic from turning configuration drift into an incident. Do not create a transformation inside an upload handler. A retryable data-plane operation and a configuration-plane write have different failure semantics, so combining them expands the blast radius: a rate limit, timeout, or duplicate delivery can now affect both the listing image and the definition meant to process it. For logistics marketplaces, where several photos may describe one shipment or item, that coupling also makes capacity planning needlessly opaque. Work backward from the page. items.title: Node.js Product Photos: Remove Backgrounds, Then Compress for Storefront Delivery
items.summary: TL;DR: Remove the background from the best available source, compress the resulting cutout for storefront delivery, and retain both the original and the cutout. Queue the pair of transformations rather than holding a Node.js upload open. For property-management teams that also extract appliance labels or inspection text with OCR, moderation coverage is a pass/fail vendor gate, while OCR must continue to use the retained original. The order is the invariant: original -> cutout -> compressed derivative. Compression before background removal gives the cutout stage a degraded input; discarding the cutout means every later compression-policy change triggers another removal operation. Those stages have different lifetimes and should not be fused. I would include Infrai in this experiment when the platform team wants the provider behind background removal or compression to change without rewriting the application contract. The primary reason is that one REST API keeps the application boundary fixed while the implementation behind a capability moves; plain HTTP means the Go worker needs no SDK. items.title: The anti-flicker tax: what hiding your page does to LCP
items.summary: If you've run a test from a visual editor, you've probably seen it: the page loads with the old headline, and a beat later the new one snaps into place. That's flicker. Client-side testing tools all have to deal with it, because their script applies the variant after the browser has started painting. From inside the browser you can either show the original and swap it, so the visitor sees the flash, or hide the page until the script is done. The second option is the "anti-flicker snippet", and most tools turn it on by default. An anti-flicker snippet makes the page invisible, usually with opacity: 0 on the body or a class like Google Optimize's async-hide. It reveals the page when the testing script finishes or a timeout fires, whichever comes first, so the timeout is your worst case. The defaults are generous: Google Optimize shipped its snippet with a 4,000 ms default (Google's developer docs). Optimize shut down on September 30, 2023, but copies of that snippet are still sitting in plenty of tags. Webflow Optimize also defaults to 4,000 ms. items.title: React Email Verification Needs Typed States
items.summary: Email verification looks like a small feature until a user clicks “send again” while a request is still running, opens an old link, or returns to the tab after the token expired. Then a simple isVerified boolean starts carrying too much meaning. I have found a cleaner approach in React projects: model the verification journey as a small, typed state machine. It gives the UI a clear answer to “what can happen next?” and gives tests a stable contract. The result is less spinner guessing, fewer impossible screens, and a signup flow that feels intentional. This is tempting: const [isVerified, setIsVerified] = useState(false); But false could mean all of these things: The user has not submitted the form. The verification request is in flight. The email was sent successfully. The request failed temporarily. The link was invalid or already used. The link expired. Those states need different copy, controls, and recovery actions. A user should not see a generic “not verified” message when the real next step is to check an inbox. The form dont need to know every backend detail, but it does need a trustworthy product state. items.title: Metering a Free Tier by Words Instead of Days in a Mac App
items.summary: On November 11, DraftKey shipped two releases about six hours apart. Version 0.1.61 made the app free to try with 2,000 words of writing help per Mac. Version 0.1.62 cut that to 500 words, added a warning when about 100 words are left, and changed what the app looks like once the allowance runs out. Both release notes are public, and they are the source for every DraftKey detail in this post. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This is not a pricing post. It is about the engineering decisions hiding behind a sentence like "every Mac gets 500 free words," because almost none of them are obvious until you have to ship one. The default trial for desktop software is a clock: 7 or 14 days, then a paywall. A clock is easy to build and easy to explain. It is also a poor match for a tool you use in short bursts. Someone installs a writing helper on a Monday, uses it twice, gets busy, and comes back on day 15 to a locked app they never really tried. items.summary: On the Events list, the browser discovered zero WebMCP tools. Opening an event draft exposed four. Switching to a trip draft replaced them with five trip tools. That route sequence is the behavior I wanted when Trip Workbench gained a second workflow. Registering every operation at startup would have exposed two unrelated domains even when only one editor was visible. Page-scoped tools make the current context clearer. They also create a design question: how does an agent enter a workflow whose tools exist only after the right page is open? The event editor has a title, date range, time zone, location mode, location label, and notes. The trip editor has airports, travel dates, cabin, traveler count, and purpose. Both workflows reuse authorization, revision, and command-receipt patterns, but they keep separate coordinators, services, tables, validation rules, policy versions, and identifiers. Event tools accept eventId; trip tools accept draftId. items.title: Volume zero is not mute
items.summary: With the volume at zero, my MacBook's speakers were still playing. Quietly enough that you only notice in a quiet room, but they were playing. On a Mac, volume and mute are two separate things. Volume is a number between 0 and 1. Mute is a switch. CoreAudio keeps them as two properties on the output device, and nothing forces them to agree. The number is a position on the device's range, and the device reports that range in decibels. So I asked the built-in speakers for theirs: var range = AudioValueRange() var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout .size) var a = AudioObjectPropertyAddress( mSelector: kAudioDevicePropertyVolumeRangeDecibels, mScope: kAudioDevicePropertyScopeOutput, mElement: kAudioObjectPropertyElementMain) AudioObjectGetPropertyData(device, &a, 0, nil, &size, &range) print(range.mMinimum, range.mMaximum) // -63.5 0.0 The bottom of the range is −63.5 dB. That is very quiet. It is not off. Usually nobody notices, because macOS flips the mute switch as well when the volume arrives at zero. items.summary: Short answer: index the caption text together with the asset ID, width, and height, then resolve each hit to a signed asset link. Do not pretend that the pixels are searchable by themselves. For a developer-tools product that smart-crops one source image into several aspect ratios, the harder decision is moderation coverage: a fast vector index does not tell you whether a generated crop is safe to show. That distinction matters during an incident. The page fires because a search result points at a crop that should not have been visible. The on-call sees a request ID, an asset ID, and a list of dimensions, but no useful explanation of why the result passed the product's policy. The alert is late because the system measured query latency, not the missing moderation decision. The first signal should be an index-policy mismatch: an asset is searchable while its current caption or moderation state is absent, stale, or tied to a different crop. items.title: Node.js RAG Benefits Over Fine-Tuning for a Changing Company Handbook
items.summary: Short answer: use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for a company handbook because the facts stay outside the model. Edit a policy, re-index its chunks, and the next retrieval can use the new text. Fine-tuning puts behavior into model weights; correcting a baked-in fact requires another training run. RAG can also return the source passage behind an answer. Fine-tuning cannot. For a fintech handbook, that distinction matters more than model novelty. Expense limits, approval chains, and compliance language change. The useful question is how quickly a changed paragraph becomes searchable without making every answer slow. My decision rule is direct: fine-tune for stable style or output format; retrieve facts that people will edit. Infrai fits one specific part of this path: OCR and vector operations share one Bearer key and one REST base URL. The second advantage is a self-describing, public discovery surface that requires no key. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. items.title: Can You Decrypt a Bcrypt Hash? No, and Here Is What Works Instead
items.summary: Every week someone asks how to "decrypt" a bcrypt hash. Here is the short answer, and what to do instead. Originally published on BcryptGenerator.org. No, a bcrypt hash can't be decrypted. Not online, not with the salt, and not with a key, because there is no key. Bcrypt is a one-way hash: it turns a password into a fixed string, and there's no operation that turns that string back. The only way to learn the password behind a bcrypt hash is to guess passwords and check each guess, and bcrypt is deliberately designed to make that slow. That's usually not what you actually need, though. Below are the things people searching "bcrypt decrypt" are usually trying to do, and how to do each one. Hashing. The difference matters: Encryption (e.g. AES) Hashing (bcrypt) Reversible? Yes, with the key No Uses a key? Yes, and it must stay secret No key at all Output Grows with the data Always 60 characters Used for Data you need to read back Passwords you only need to check Encryption is for things your program must read back later, like a stored API token. Passwords should never be stored that way; OWASP's Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends hashing them with a slow algorithm such as Argon2i

items.title: Node.js SaaS App Weekly Support — Background Job Queue, HTTP Workers, Retries, DLQ
items.summary: Short answer: put each weekly customer-support digest on a background job queue, make the Node.js worker idempotent, and use cron only to enqueue the scheduled work. Choose by the cost of recovering one failed digest, not by the cost of one queue operation. The constraint is awkward but decisive: a cron run can call only a public http_url and stops at 900 seconds. A weekly batch for active customers can outgrow that window, especially when rendering, email delivery, and webhook calls share the same run. Queueing separates the clock from the work, so retries and a dead-letter queue (DLQ) remain available after the scheduler has moved on. For a small support SaaS, I would try Infrai for the enqueue-and-worker boundary when reducing operational glue matters: one key and one bill cover its backend capabilities, and the plain REST surface doesn't require another Node.js SDK. That's a narrow recommendation. The queue earns its place through a shorter recovery path, while the consolidated account and HTTP integration reduce the surrounding work. Write the recovery invariant before comparing products: one failed customer digest must be retryable without resending any completed digest. Mode

items.title: Why a Mac Writing Helper Needs Two Permissions, and Why It Still Refuses Password Fields
items.summary: A writing helper that works inside someone else's text field has to ask macOS for a lot of trust. Accessibility permission is how an app reads and, if you approve it, replaces text in another app. Input Monitoring is how it can see keyboard events while you are in Mail, Notes, or a browser. Those are two different Privacy & Security toggles, and they should be. People are right to pause on both. We build DraftKey, a Mac app for Tab autocomplete and rewrites you review before they are inserted. This post is about the permission model behind a helper like that: why two system permissions are required, how we ask for them, and the cases we refuse even after you have said yes. The general mechanics come from Apple's public documentation, linked at the end. The product rules come from the shipped app's own wording, including the Apps & privacy section in Settings. Apple documents these as separate resources, and System Settings treats them that way. Accessibility is under Privacy & Security. items.title: The progress bar that made typing lag: debugging a 331 ms INP in a React game
items.summary: TL;DR: A friend told me that typing felt laggy in Museek, my free multiplayer music quiz. I was sure the culprit was my autocomplete filtering. The profiler disagreed. The real problem was a progress bar animating its width once per second, plus a full-screen backdrop-filter: blur(). Switching the bar to transform cut background Rendering time by roughly 7x and took keystrokes out of the slow interactions list. Museek is a browser-based "blind test": up to 12 players each bring a Spotify, Deezer or Apple Music playlist, a song snippet plays, and everyone types the artist and title as fast as they can. It's built with Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind 4, with a Node/Socket.io backend. A friend playing a game sent me this: "There's a delay between what I type and what shows up in the answer field." In a game where you're racing a 30-second timer, that's not a cosmetic issue. Each answer field has an autocomplete. On every render, my Game component filtered the whole song and artist database, and called a fairly expensive normalizeString() (Unicode NFD normalization plus two regexes) twice per item. items.title: Formik vs React Hook Form: Which One Should You Choose for Your React Projects?
items.summary: When working with React, forms are something you will deal with in almost every project. Whether you're building a login page, registration form, admin dashboard, job application portal, e-commerce checkout, or a multi-step form, managing form data and validation can quickly become complicated. Initially, handling forms using React's useState seems straightforward. But as the application grows, things get messy. You start dealing with: Managing multiple input values. Handling validation for every field. Displaying error messages. Tracking touched and dirty fields. Managing form submission. Handling API errors. Preventing unnecessary re-renders. Supporting dynamic fields and complex validations. This is where form management libraries become useful. Two popular choices in the React ecosystem are React Hook Form and Formik. I've worked with both approaches, and one thing I've noticed is that choosing a form library isn't just about writing fewer lines of code. It's also about understanding how it manages form state and how that affects your application. items.title: Monolith, Modular Monolith and Microservices: A Practical Comparison for .NET
items.summary: Cover photo by Nicolás Gutiérrez on Unsplash Most software engineers do not choose their architecture in a vacuum. You usually meet architectures in stages: traditional monoliths in legacy codebases or early-stage products, microservices when a company wants independent team scaling, and modular monoliths when an organization realizes that distributed systems introduce operational costs they did not anticipate. Each approach is often marketed as the obvious successor to the one before it. In real engineering, however, these architectures are simply points on a trade-off spectrum balancing operational simplicity against structural isolation. This article compares traditional monoliths, modular monoliths, and microservices across core architectural dimensions, outlines the specific .NET libraries and frameworks each one relies on, and provides practical criteria for choosing between them. items.title: Crediting MT5 trading accounts from Indonesian QRIS and virtual account deposits, exactly once
items.summary: By William Beaumont, Head of Operations at PAYJN A client in Jakarta opens your broker's cashier, picks "Bank transfer (VA)", pays IDR 5,000,000 from their mobile banking app and switches back to MetaTrader. Somewhere between the bank, the payment provider, your webhook endpoint and your back office, that payment has to become a balance operation on exactly one trading account, once. Many deposit problems in a broker cashier are not payment failures. The money arrived, but the system credited it twice, credited the wrong account, or never credited it at all because one step assumed another had already done its job. This article walks through a deposit design for Indonesian QRIS and virtual account (VA) payments that avoids those three outcomes. The code is illustrative Node.js with invented field names. It is not any provider's API, and mt5.balance / mt5.findBalanceDeal stand for your own wrapper around the MT5 Manager or server API. Double credit. The provider retries a webhook because your acknowledgement timed out, or two workers process the same event at once, and both post a balance operation to MT5. Wrong account. items.title: Docker's agent sandbox leaked through its copy command. Check every path that crosses the wall.
items.summary: Originally published on voirlabs.io by Ijlal Ishaq. A sandbox for an AI agent is only as strong as the least guarded way in or out of it. Docker Sandboxes put a coding agent in its own virtual machine and let it see only the folders you approve, and that part held. The gap was the copy command next to it. By the end of this article you will know why that keeps happening, and what a file channel that respects the boundary looks like in code. Docker Sandboxes runs agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI inside a microVM with its own kernel, filesystem and network. You grant it specific folders, usually the project workspace, and those folders are shared into the VM. Together they form an allowlist: the only parts of your machine the agent is supposed to reach. On November 3, Peyton Kennedy of Endor Labs published CVE-2026-103916, a flaw he found in sbx cp, the command that moves files between the sandbox and your machine. The copy runs on your side, with your permissions, and never consults the allowlist. In Kennedy's words, the CLI "resolves symlinks in the paths it is given and acts on the resolution." items.title: Virtual try-on with a one-image edit model: collage, edit in place, crop
items.summary: A virtual try-on needs two pictures: a photo of the person and a photo of the garment. The image endpoint we run our standard model on accepts exactly one input image. We didn't want to change that endpoint, or the API contract our mobile app depends on, just to add a feature to the website. The workaround turned out to be simple, and one detail in it made the difference between a feature that works most of the time and one that works every time we tried it. The client builds a single image: the person on the left, the garment on the right on a plain light background, like a product shot. The pair is 1024 pixels tall, so the person keeps the same resolution as a normal single-photo edit. The tricky part is the shape. The edit model only produces a fixed set of aspect ratios (1:1, 4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16 and their landscape versions). If the collage doesn't match one of them exactly, the model pads or crops it, and the person ends up shifted or squeezed. items.title: Shipping 52 Releases of a Mac App: What Signed Updates Have to Get Right
items.summary: Your first auto-update is a promise. Your second one is where you find out whether you kept it. We build DraftKey, a small Mac app for Tab autocomplete and reviewed rewrites. Between September 20 and November 11, 2026 we tagged 52 public releases on GitHub, from 0.1.1 to 0.1.62. That is a lot of updates to push at people who installed a writing tool and mostly want it to stay out of the way. This post is about the boring plumbing that made that pace survivable, and the one early bug that forced users to reinstall by hand. Everything about DraftKey below comes from our public release notes. The general mechanics come from Apple's and the Sparkle project's public documentation, linked at the end. If you ship a Mac app outside the App Store, most of this applies to you whatever updater you use. The 0.1.1 notes are short, and every line is a rule we still follow: You can check for and install signed updates from the menu bar or from Settings, under About. Automatic update checks can be turned off. Installing an update requires your approval. Updates preserve your license, your preferences, and the downloaded writing model. items.title: "Failed" Is a Lie Your .NET Agent Tells the Model: Four Outcomes Every Tool Call Needs
items.summary: Most tool functions I see in agent demos return one of two things: a result, or an exception. Microsoft.Extensions.AI then turns that exception into a polite little string for the model, something like Error: Function failed. For a read, that's fine. For a write, it's a trap. Picture a refund tool. The HTTP call to billing goes out, billing commits the refund, and the response gets lost on the way back. Your timeout fires. The tool throws. The model reads "failed", does the helpful thing, and calls the refund tool again. The customer is now 40 EUR richer instead of 20. The model didn't misbehave. You told it something false. It had no way to know "failed" really meant "I have no idea". This post is about the small vocabulary I now give every tool in a .NET agent so the model never has to guess. items.title: Merging PDF and DOCX in .NET: The Proper In-Memory Approach Without MS Office or Temporary Files
items.summary: Consider a typical business scenario: you need to generate a final report for a client and deliver it as a single file. This report is compiled from various sources: A dynamic cover page (generated as a DOCX file from a template). Analytics, including charts (exported as a PDF from a third-party BI tool). A standard legal appendix (a static PDF). Your task as a developer is to seamlessly merge these into a single, final PDF file and deliver it to the user via an HTTP response. Common approaches to this problem in .NET often lead to complications: Microsoft Office Interop: Does not work in Linux/Docker environments and frequently causes memory leaks or orphaned WINWORD.EXE processes. Temporary files: Writing individual documents to disk, merging them, and then deleting them creates I/O bottlenecks, file-locking issues, and security risks. Naive byte concatenation: Simply joining byte[] arrays together will inevitably result in a corrupted, unreadable file. items.summary: Integrating a payment gateway into an application often means dealing with HTTP requests, authentication, JSON serialization, API response formats, and transaction verification. For .NET developers integrating with PayChangu, I wanted to make that experience a little easier. That is why I built PayChangu.NET — an open-source .NET SDK that provides a strongly typed, asynchronous interface for interacting with the PayChangu payment gateway. Instead of writing HTTP requests and manually handling API responses for every payment operation, you can use familiar C# classes, methods, and dependency injection. In this article, I'll walk through what PayChangu.NET offers, how to install and configure it, and how to use it to integrate different PayChangu payment flows into a .NET application. PayChangu.NET is an open-source .NET SDK for the PayChangu payment gateway. It is designed to simplify communication with PayChangu's APIs by providing: Strongly typed request and response models. items.title: app_offline.htm in ASP.NET Core: How It Works and Why It Fails
items.summary: You copy a new build of your ASP.NET Core app to IIS and the copy fails half-way: "The process cannot access the file 'MyApp.dll' because it is being used by another process." Someone on Stack Overflow says "use app_offline.htm". You drop the file in, and either nothing changes, or the site shows a blank page, or IIS's own 503 page, or it stays offline after you deleted the file. app_offline.htm is a small feature with very little documentation. Microsoft's page on it is about 360 words and doesn't even say which status code it returns. Most of what you find on blogs and forums was written for classic ASP.NET on IIS 7, and some of it, like "the file must be at least 512 bytes", is wrong for ASP.NET Core. So for this guide I read the source of the ASP.NET Core Module (ANCM), the IIS module that implements the feature, and checked each rule against it. Every fact below links to the line it comes from. I also use the file on every deploy of this site's own API, an ASP.NET Core 9 app running in-process on shared Windows hosting with Plesk, so the deploy sections are the steps I actually run, including the one that cost me 40 uploaded images. Short version: put a file named app_offline.

items.title: FAA Expands AI Advice to Manage Air Traffic Congestion Across Entire US Airspace
items.summary: The FAA is expanding its $875 million AI-powered SMART system to all 22 U.S. air traffic control centers across the country. Since being implemented over Washington, DC, on September 21, the system has helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. Ars Technica reports: The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about "weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics" to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft. However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency. Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system "cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft," the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. items.title: Euclid Mission Data Release Spans More Than 900 Million Galaxies
items.summary: The European Space Agency has released the largest dataset yet from its Euclid space telescope, containing 1.7 petabytes of observations covering more than 900 million galaxies. "The data unveiled on Thursday covered a survey of the sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the moon as viewed from Earth," reports Reuters. items.title: What it takes to turn an iPhone microphone into a decibel meter
items.summary: I work on Noise Meter at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that shows the sound level in decibels and logs a whole night of it, so someone with a noisy neighbour can show when it was loud. This post is about the measuring part: what happens between the microphone and the number on screen, and the places where I had to be honest about what a phone can't do. iOS processes microphone input by default: automatic gain, noise suppression, EQ. All of that is exactly what a meter must not have, because a quiet room would be boosted and a loud one pulled down. The audio session mode that turns it off is .measurement: try session.setCategory(.record, mode: .measurement) try session.setPreferredSampleRate(48_000) From there it is an AVAudioEngine input tap with a 4800-frame buffer, which is 100 ms at 48 kHz. I ask for 48 kHz but build the analyzer for whatever rate the hardware returns. I also select the built-in microphone's bottom data source with an omnidirectional pattern, and re-select it on every route change, because a route change can move the input. items.title: I built an iOS app where your documents delete themselves
items.summary: We keep too many documents forever. Scans of contracts, tickets, IDs sent for a one-time procedure, a rental agreement from three years ago. Most of them only matter for a short time, and then they just sit in your phone, your cloud and your photo library, waiting to be leaked, lost or forgotten. So I built Fadely: an iOS app that works as a vault for temporary documents. You add a document, choose a date, and when that date arrives the document destroys itself. My brother-in-law flies constantly. His passport was buried among hundreds of downloads on his phone, and he always worried: what if it gets stolen? So in Fadely, docs get an expiry date. Then they're gone for good. 🔒 Most storage apps are built on one assumption: keep everything, forever. Fadely does the opposite. Every document has an expiry date from the moment you save it. You decide how long it should exist, and the app takes care of the rest. items.title: What It Takes to Put Tab Autocomplete Inside Other Apps' Text Fields on macOS
items.summary: Autocomplete inside your own text view is a solved problem. You own the NSTextView, you know where the caret is, and you decide what Tab does. Autocomplete inside someone else's text field, in an app you did not write, is a different job. You don't own the text, the caret, or the Tab key. You borrow all three through macOS Accessibility, and each app lends them a little differently. We build DraftKey, a Mac app that suggests the rest of your sentence as you type and adds it when you press Tab. This post is about the plumbing behind that kind of feature. For the general mechanics I'm citing Apple's public documentation. For what we actually ran into, I'm citing our own public release notes: 52 tagged releases on GitHub, from 0.1.1 on September 20 to 0.1.62 on November 11, 2026. When I'm describing the macOS API surface in general rather than DraftKey's code, I'll say so. A Mac app can't read another app's text fields by default. It has to be a trusted accessibility client, and only the user can grant that. items.title: Four lessons from building a handwriting notes app for iPad
items.summary: I've been building GraphNotes, a notes app for iPad, iPhone Duo, and Mac where handwriting, PDF highlights and typed notes share one library. Two rules shaped most of its technical decisions: The ink is the note. The app reads your handwriting so it can search it, but it never swaps your strokes for its guess at what they say. Every thought keeps its way back. A note written beside a highlighted passage stays linked to that exact passage, and links point at permanent IDs, never at titles. It's built with SwiftUI (and UIKit where touch handling needs it), PencilKit, SQLite (libSQL through a fork of GRDB) and CloudKit's CKSyncEngine. Here are four things that took me longer to get right than I expected, in case they save you some time. It's tempting to spot new strokes by comparing drawing.strokes.count. Undo, redo and the vector eraser all break that. What works is diffing the strokes of two states by PKStrokePath.creationDate, the wall-clock time the pen touched down. The object is at the centre of a galaxy known as M87, about 55 million light-years away. The iconic ring structure instantly became one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. It showed a black hole "shadow" outlined by light from swirling hot gas -- just as predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity. The result supported the long-standing idea that the centers of galaxies house supermassive black holes. However, scientists have since had some disagreements on whether the details and structure of the ring in the original publication were accurate. Our new research, published today in Nature, used new techniques to investigate the original datasets. Not only do our results validate the original work, but they also provide a fresh perspective on the ring structure. items.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
items.summary: A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code and potentially take control of affected server processes. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, the vulnerability affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when HTTP/2 is enabled and is fixed in version 2.4.71. The Hacker News reports: The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported. HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: Swarm (/swarm) (10 minute read)
items.summary: The /swarm command in Google Antigravity runs a team of named agents that split tasks, work on the pieces at the same time, and coordinate on one shared message board. It can be used for tasks that divide cleanly across separate files, packages, or questions, or when a second agent is needed to review and test the changes before a human sees it. items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: Harness 2: executing agent code as it streams (6 minute read)
items.summary: Framer's Harness 2 significantly upgrades the agent's execution process, allowing entire workflows in one program, achieving up to 33% cost reduction and 20% faster execution. The redesign also replaces DSL with method calls for real-time updates, making task execution streamlined for both in-app and external agents, reducing tool steps by 43% and cached input tokens by 39% per message.

items.summary: Swarms are AI systems where multiple agents cooperate towards a shared goal. This post discusses a technique called collective inference-time scaling, where agents scale the amount of useful work performed in parallel and the communication needed to achieve it. It also explains how to design incentives for parallel work, and covers the general topic of designing incentives for reinforcement learning.

items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)
items.summary: Agents are collapsing their entire tool catalog into one 'exec' tool. This allows models to write short scripts that chain, combine, and await actions inside isolated sandboxes. Models can now reliably combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass. In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.
